short: The fall of England's last continental possession, ending its mainland European presence.
full:
On 7 January 1558, the French army under the Duke of Guise captured Calais, bringing an end to more than two centuries of English rule. Calais had been conquered by Edward III in 1347 and stood as England's final territorial holding on the European continent. Queen Mary I had drawn England into the Italian War of 1551–1559 to support her husband, Philip II of Spain, leaving the heavily fortified but poorly garrisoned pale of Calais vulnerable to a surprise winter assault.

The loss was a profound psychological and strategic blow to the English establishment. It deprived English merchants of a vital staple port for the wool trade and eliminated a crucial military bridgehead into northern Europe. Although Mary famously reportedly claimed that the word "Calais" would be found engraved on her heart upon her death, her successor Elizabeth I eventually abandoned efforts to recapture the town. The surrender finalized England's reorientation away from continental European expansion and towards maritime power and Atlantic exploration.
